          Listener rules

          Listener rules determine how connection requests received by the load balancer are routed, using the conditions and actions that you configure.

          Conditions are specific parameters a request must match for the rules actions to be performed. Rules can have a single condition, or a series of conditions, but requests must match all specified conditions for the action to be performed.

          A rule can include one of each of the following conditions: host-header, path-pattern, http-request-method and source-ip.

          A rule can include one or more of each of the following conditions: http-header and query-string.

          Each rule must include exactly one of the following actions: Forward, Redirect, or Fixed-response, and it must be the last action to be performed.

          For HTTPS listeners, you can include Authenticate as an action with Amazon Cognito or OpenID Connect (OIDC).

          A Forward action routes requests to one or more target groups. With forward actions, you can assign a weight that controls the prioritization and selection of each target group. Weights must be set as an integer between 0 and 999.

          Redirect actions are used to redirect client requests from one URL to another. You must modify at least one of the following: protocol, hostname, port, or path, to avoid a redirect loop. Any components that you don't modify retain their original values.

          You can use Fixed-response actions to drop client requests and return a custom HTTP response. You can use this action to return a 2XX, 4XX, or 5XX response code and add an optional message.

          When a request is received by a listener with multiple rules, the order in which the rules are evaluated is determined by each rule's priority. You can change the priority of any rule at any time, except the listener's default rule, which is always evaluated last.

          A rule's priority can be set between 1-50000. Rules cannot have the same priority.

          Rules are evaluated in order from the lowest value, to the highest value. So a rule with a priority of 5 will be evaluated before a rule with a priority of 10.
